title: Compliments from listeners and Europeans who know New Orleans
summary: An old Black man at a street dance said the white band made the 'darkest music'; a Cuban waiter compared him to Jack Carey; Europeans asked about George Lewis and Al Hirt.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Hmm. Well, one more thing I wanted to ask you about was that compliment you told me you got.

Oh, yeah. Uh, yeah, it seems that just before we went to York, we were playing a street dance in order to raise funds for our trip, see? So, in this particular neighborhood that we were playing is, well, it's predominantly a colored section. So, they had one old colored fella, he was hanging by the rope, you see? We had this area roped off and he was hanging back there by the rope, doing a jig and a dance out in the street, see? So, when we had an intermission, I walked over to the rope and was talking to him, and he told me, he says, uh, you know, he says, for white fellas, y'all play the darkest music I ever heard. And naturally, we are trying to reproduce that old Negro sound, and to me, that was a great compliment, you know, because that's what we want to do. Yeah, he says, for a white group, y'all make the darkest music I ever heard.
Oh, what did that guy say to you at the, what was it, the Yacht Club or the Country Club? Uh, that guy, the waiter comes up to you and plays you a high compliment, remember? The guy from Cuba?
He said, I sound just like, uh, Big Chief, huh?
He said, I play that just like, uh, Jacare. I play that part in that tune just like Jacare. Jacare. Jacare.
That guy had come over from Cuba when?

Um, well, you know, it's surprising how many of these people that come from other places know so much about, uh, you know, about, uh, Dixie Lounge. Uh, when we were over in Europe, uh, all these people would come up to us and they'd ask us if we knew, uh, George Lewis, uh, do we know Lawrence Marrera, do we know Al Hurt, and, uh, for the sake of a joke, I told them, I said, well, I taught Al Hurt to play a horn. And, uh, golly, I'd never seen Al, uh, I wish I had the opportunity to meet him. I like him, you see, but I'd never seen, I'd never seen Al play. And, uh, these people just thought that was something, you know, until I had to let them on that I was just joking, you know. I don't think there's another Al Hurt in the country, boy.
